questions.q: What is the standard way modern Salesforce API clients authenticate?
options: OAuth 2.0, obtaining a short-lived access token and sending it as a Bearer token on every call
Sending a raw username and password on every single API call
No authentication is required for REST or Bulk API calls
A permanent, never-expiring API key issued once per org
questions.explain: OAuth 2.0 access tokens, obtained through one of several flows, are the standard authentication mechanism across Salesforce's modern APIs.

questions.q: Which OAuth flow is correct for a fully automated, server-to-server integration with no human user present to approve access?
options: The Web Server (Authorization Code) flow
The JWT Bearer flow
The Device Flow
The legacy Username-Password flow, which Salesforce recommends for all new server integrations
questions.explain: The JWT Bearer flow signs a JWT assertion with a private key and exchanges it directly for an access token, with no browser redirect or user approval step.

questions.q: What is changing in 2026 regarding how new OAuth client apps are registered in Salesforce?
options: Nothing has changed; Connected Apps remain the only way to register a client
Salesforce has disabled creating new Connected Apps across all orgs, recommending the newer External Client App (ECA) instead — existing Connected Apps still work
OAuth has been removed entirely in favor of raw API keys
Only SOAP API clients can now be registered; REST clients no longer need registration
questions.explain: Winter '26 and Spring '26 extended a block on new Connected App creation to all orgs, with External Client Apps as the new recommended registration object — existing Connected Apps were not deprecated.

questions.q: In the Web Server (Authorization Code) flow, what does the app exchange at /services/oauth2/token to get an access token?
options: The user's raw password
A short-lived authorization code it received after the user approved access
A WSDL file
A SOQL query string
questions.explain: After the user approves access, Salesforce redirects back with a short-lived authorization code, which the app then exchanges for an access token (and refresh token) at the token endpoint.

questions.q: Why does this lesson advise against building new integrations on the legacy Username-Password OAuth flow?
options: It has already been completely removed from Salesforce with no warning
It only works with the GraphQL API
Salesforce is actively retiring it (targeted for Winter '27) and discourages it for new integrations
It requires a JWT assertion, which makes it more complex than other flows
questions.explain: The Username-Password flow sends raw credentials to the token endpoint and is being phased out by Salesforce — new integrations should use a flow like Web Server or JWT Bearer instead.
